case_studies.title: Rubric-Calibrated Preferences: Cross-Query Calibration of LLM Judgments via Item Response Theory
case_studies.abstract: Rerankers decide which documents users and LLMs see, yet their standard metric, nDCG, relies on human relevance labels that are costly, sparse, noisy, and discretely graded. As rerankers approach each other in quality, nDCG on these labels therefore increasingly fails to separate them. LLM judges could supply dense labels. Relative judgments within one query tell even close candidates apart, yet their scores share no scale across queries. Absolute grades share one scale but are too coarse to distinguish documents of similar relevance. We propose Rubric-Calibrated Preferences (RCP), which combi
case_studies.summary: The paper proposes a method to calibrate large‑language‑model judgments so that relative and absolute relevance scores can be compared across different search queries. It builds a system that blends relative rankings within a query with a shared absolute scale, using Item Response Theory to produce dense, comparable relevance labels. The result is higher‑quality reranking that better separates similar‑quality systems, but it does not directly impact cloud infrastructure management.
case_studies.it_breakdown: Not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper proposes a method (Rubric‑Calibrated Preferences) to calibrate LLM‑based judgments for document reranking. It presents a new way to generate dense relevance labels that could improve ranking in enterprise search or recommendation systems. While the idea is novel, it is fairly academic and does not provide immediate, actionable tools. IT engineers could use the concept to build or improve internal search pipelines, but practical implementation would require significant engineering effort. It has moderate relevance to LLM APIs and retrieval systems, but limited direct applicability in the next 90 days. The total score exceeds 40, so the signal is not marked as low.

case_studies.title: From Migration to Calibration: Preserving Agent Capabilities across Models, Jurisdictions, and Scale
case_studies.abstract: Agents need calibration when deployment conditions change: replacing a driving model, including a foundation-to-post-trained transition; crossing jurisdictions; or scaling across heterogeneous markets and sources. Interface compatibility alone does not establish capability retention or target-contract satisfaction. We formulate agent calibration as constrained behavioral adaptation across three interacting layers: information preservation, harness adaptation, and user acceptance; the layers apply to every scenario, not one-to-one to the three. The basic objective is non-degradation on prespeci
case_studies.summary: This research tackles the loss of an AI agent’s performance when you switch models, move across legal boundaries, or scale to new markets. The authors built a three‑layer calibration framework—information preservation, harness adaptation, and user acceptance—to keep agent behaviour on target. The result is a method that can help you keep your deployed AI services running consistently under change.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage cloud AI deployments, apply the framework: 1) map all data flows and model inputs to preserve information integrity; 2) adjust your infrastructure harness (e.g., API gateways, scaling policies) to match the new model’s requirements; 3) run user‑acceptance tests to confirm performance meets contractual SLAs. If your org doesn’t use AI agents, this is not directly applicable.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper discusses calibration of AI agents across different models and deployment contexts, which could inform engineers working with LLM APIs and scaling across cloud regions. However, it offers limited actionable guidance for immediate implementation, so the value within 90 days is modest.

case_studies.title: Semantics, Workflows, and Infrastructure: Understanding Agent Serving at Production Scale
case_studies.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents execute applications through a workflow of inference requests with tool calls and user interactions. Serving these applications at production scale requires understanding how application behavior shapes inference demand and for guiding efficient execution. Recent characterization studies provide request-level workload measurements and agent execution analysis. However, an end-to-end view connecting task initiation, workflow execution, and inference infrastructure remains unexplored. case_studies.summary: This research looks at how large language model agents use cloud infrastructure by tracking every inference request in a real‑world workflow. The authors analysed a two‑week trace of 11.7 million requests to map the whole cycle from task start to tool calls and user replies, uncovering patterns that can optimise resource usage. The result is a clearer picture of demand spikes and bottlenecks, enabling more efficient scaling of LLM services.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage cloud infrastructure for LLM services, first map your own request flow like the authors did; second, identify peak demand periods and tool‑call patterns; third, adjust autoscaling and caching policies to align with those patterns for cost savings and improved latency.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper provides an end‑to‑end view of LLM agent workloads and infrastructure, offering insights that could influence how IT engineers plan scaling and resource allocation for LLM‑based services. However, the findings are largely analytical with limited immediate buildable actions, resulting in a modest value score.
